title: Learning Global Probabilistic Explanations
claim: Our spectral method reaches optimal error within the theoretical bound and query budget, while the greedy baseline fails on adversarial targets.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row; dashed theory bounds overlaid; panel titles below
description: Three side-by-side line plots with error bars compare a greedy explainer (GE, red squares) with a spectral explainer (SE, blue circles) on synthetic targets. Panel (a), 'Synergy Trap', plots error against explanation size k from 2 to 5. GE error climbs from 0 to 0.25, with a large error bar at k=3. SE stays flat at 0, on the dotted optimum line. Panel (b), 'Noisy parity: gap', plots excess error against epsilon from 0.20 to 0.45. SE stays at 0, while GE sits around 0.37–0.41 with tall error bars and often exceeds the dashed green epsilon bound. Panel (c), 'Noisy parity: queries', is a log-scale plot of membership queries against epsilon. SE tracks the dashed green analytic bound (2d+1)bn, falling from about 1e10 to 5e8, while GE uses far fewer queries, around 2e5. The eye goes first to the red GE curves diverging from the flat blue SE line.
caption: Synthetic targets (d = 16); bars show the range over runs. (a) errf,D(K) against k, with opt = 0. (b) errf,D(K) −opt against ϵ, with the bound ϵ (dashed). (c) Membership queries against ϵ, with the value (2d + 1) b n of the analysis (dashed).
abstract: Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence. While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution. Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$. In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces. We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations. Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.
